What the heck is causal inference?

  • This is a class about causal inference
  • Wikipedia Definition
    • Causal Inference is the process of determining the independent, actual effect of a particular phenomenon that is a component of a larger system.
    • This means moving past simple correlations to find what causes what
    • Effective causal inference methods can be difficult to implement, but can offer compelling evidence

Causal Inference

  • We know that \[Correlation \neq Causation\]
  • So what does equal causation??

Causal Inference

  • It turns out that
  • \[Correlation + Assumptions = Causation\]

Causal Inference (cont’d)

  • Most interesting questions require causal inference:
  • Why are these hard questions to answer?
    • Does getting more sleep make you earn more money? (Costa-Font et al, (2024))
    • Does getting diagnosed with Diabetes cause people to adopt healthier habits? (Alalouf et al (2024))
    • Are judges harsher on juveniles when their favorite football team loses? (Eren and Mocan (2017))

Interest in causal inference is growing

How did I do that?

library(tidyverse)
google_trends <- read.csv("google_trends_causal_inf_2025.csv") %>%
  mutate(date = as.Date(paste(year,month,15,sep="-")))

causal_inf_graph <- ggplot(google_trends, aes(x=date,y=interest)) + 
  geom_point() + 
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = TRUE, color = "darkgray") +
  ylab("Interest") + 
  xlab("Date") + 
  theme_classic() + 
   theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, face = "bold")) +
  ggtitle("Google Trends Interest in 'Causal Inference'")

Here’s the result

Why is Causal Inference Hard?

  • We have unprecedented amounts of data
  • Lots of tools at our disposal

The Experimental Ideal

  • Randomized Controlled Trials (RCT) are considered the gold standard in causal inference

    • Why is that?

What is an RCT?

  • Let’s say you have a new miracle drug that you think will cure halitosis (bad breath) in all humans.
  • How can you prove it works?
    • Recruit a bunch of participants with bad breath
    • Want to give drug to some and a placebo to others
    • How do we decide who gets the drug?

Randomization is the Secret Sauce

  • If you randomly choose who to give the drug to, the only difference between the two groups is the treatment!
  • Otherwise, there can always be another explanation
    • What if we gave the drug to the people with the worst breath?
    • The best breath (among the bad breath group)
    • Just the men?
  • All of these strategies open up back doors which can prevent us from drawing causal conclusions

What do we mean by back door?

  • A back door is another explanation for why outcomes diverged between the treatment and control groups
  • When the groups are different in many ways, there are lots of back doors
  • Example: does getting more education lead to higher wages?
    • What are the back doors here?

Randomization closes back doors

  • Randomization guarantees that our treated group looks just like our control group
  • But how?
  • LLN
  • Need a large enough sample
  • Can even check to make sure randomization worked

With an RCT, we don’t need fancy econometrics

  • All the hard work is done up front
  • Usually just a simple regression
  • Bannerjee and Duflo, John List, and many others do great experiments
  • Why not use RCTs for everything then?

Limitations of RCTs

  • Not always feasible ($$$)
  • Not always ethical
  • People act differently in experiments
    • Participant bias
    • Social desirability bias
  • May not be generalizable to other populations

Wrapping up RCTs

  • Despite limitations, RCTs are the gold standard
  • Provide convincing evidence that a treatment caused an outcome
  • Help policymakers make informed decisions
  • Even when RCT is not feasible, it is usually worth thinking about what kind of experiment you would run if you had unlimited funds and no moral compass

So how do we do causal inference with no RCT?

  • With no RCT, we often try to find settings where treatment ends up getting assigned in a relatively random way.
  • Often called natural experiments
  • Like RCTs, these have benefits and drawbacks

Natural experiments - benefits

  • Free from the biases that exist in RCTs
  • Allow us to answer questions that would be impossible to do an RCT on
  • Can sometimes be more generalizable
  • Involve observational data from the real world

Natural experiments - drawbacks

  • Selection bias
  • Omitted variable bias
  • Reverse causality
  • Correlation \(\neq\) causation

This class is all about how we can overcome these issues by being clever with data

Strategies for making causal claims with no RCT

  • Controlling for omitted variables
  • Differences-in-differences
  • Instrumental variables
  • Regression discontinuity

Many others, but these are the big ones

Our plans

For each of these strategies, we will learn:

  • Why they allow us to make causal claims
  • The assumptions we need to make in order to do so
  • How to implement them in R

We will start by building intuition, then focus on mechanics

Starting with a research question

  • Before we can use these methods, we need a research question
  • What makes a good research question?
    • Something that can be answered with the right data
    • If answered, it should teach us something interesting about the world

Which of these satisfies both requirements?

  • Are there more male surgeons than female surgeons?
  • Do med school professors intentionally discourage women from becoming surgeons?
  • Are female surgeons punished more harshly than male surgeons for making mistakes?*

*See Sarsons (2017) for the answer

So how do we come up with good research questions?

  • If you figure this out, let me know!
  • Good questions can come from many sources:
    • Newspapers and local news
    • Other research (pick a field journal)
    • Conferences
    • Maybe you have a cool dataset
    • Hear about a nice natural experiment

Reason we focus on intuition in this class is that I want you to build an internal radar that goes off when you hear about something that could be a nice research design

Where can we get data to answer our questions?

  • Publicly available data (see class website)
  • Replication packages (AEA papers)
  • Restricted-access data (Census, NCHS, etc.)
  • Create your own!
    • Merging datasets together
    • Google Trends, Twitter
    • Web-scraping

R - What is it good for?

We will be using R exclusively in this class

  • Why R and not STATA?
    • STATA useful in academic economics, but almost nowhere else
    • R is more versatile and growing rapidly
    • R is open-source (free)
    • R is much better at working with the internet (scraping, R-Shiny)

R Studio

R Studio is an application that makes it much easier to use R
